China thermal coal import outlook and Indonesian supply assumptions Elevated Asian freight rates redirect Latin American PP flows, opening US arbitrage Marine insurance supply remains stable as geopolitical and technical changes reshape the market, says IUMI President Orlen and Port of Gdynia to assess LNG and bio-LNG bunkering potential in Port News 08/09/2026 Polish refiner Orlen has partnered with the Port of Gdynia Authority to assess the potential for LNG and bio-LNG bunkering at the Polish port. The cooperation will examine market demand, the potential development of LNG and bio-LNG bunkering services, and the infrastructure, operational conditions and regulatory requirements needed to support them. The parties will also assess the bunkering requirements of shipowners and port users, particularly operators of scheduled ferry, container and ro-ro services. The study will consider potential bunkering models and draw on solutions already implemented at other European ports. Among the options under review will be ship-to-ship bunkering and its suitability for larger vessels, as well as the feasibility of bunkering vessels while they are alongside, including simultaneously with cargo-handling operations. “The cooperation with the Port of Gdynia marks an important step in developing the LNG and bio-LNG market in the Tricity area and forms part of a wider transformation of ORLEN’s fuel portfolio through 2035,” Orlen’s vice president Robert Soszyński said. The partnership follows Orlen’s commissioning in August of its Marine Transshipment Terminal at the Gdańsk refinery. The terminal began operations with the loading of marine gas oil (MGO) from the refinery and the delivery of fatty acid methyl ester (FAME) for biofuel production. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr93.text: Figure caption, Watch: The scene at Riyadh international airport after strike By Tinshui Yeung Published 33 minutes ago An international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh has been hit by a second strike in as many days, officials have said. A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said there had been injuries. It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week. The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace. The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours. They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said. He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa. On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4. US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia. Riyadh airport attack another dangerous moment in already tense conflict Published 1 hour ago Saturday's strike was the deadliest single attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war between Israel, the US and Iran began in February. The Saudi-led coalition vowed to respond, calling it a "war crime". Four Saudi nationals, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt were among the dead, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian man had succumbed to the injuries he sustained in the attack. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks and confirmed that a US citizen was killed in the strikes. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled". The UK Foreign Office is advising against all travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including areas within 10km (6.2 miles) of the border with Yemen, while other western embassies have warned their nationals about travel in the region. Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said "the Saudi enemy" had launched an air strike on Sanaa International Airport in Yemen's capital. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the attack and the BBC has been unable to verify this claim. Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir, vice-president of Yemen's internationally recognised government, called for "decisive actions" from regional and international partners. Riyadh's airport was struck on Thursday, an attack that killed three Saudi nationals . The Houthis claimed responsibility and said they had used cruise missiles to target the airport. There were two other deadly attacks on Saudi airports in Abha and Riyadh in the two days prior to that. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Smoke and flames seen at King Khalid airport in Riyadh on 8 October The latest uptick in violence comes after a temporary ceasefire between the Houthis and Saudi-led forces, brokered in 2022, collapsed in July. The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive, prompting Saudi strikes. Yemeni pro-government forces later said they had secured the regions. The Houthis currently control around a quarter of Yemeni territory and as much as 80% of the country's population. The Iran-backed armed group hopes to eventually seize complete control. Saudi Arabia fears this would lead to the establishment of an Iranian satellite state on its southern border. https://www.dw.com/en/poland-reports-arr.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OBb8 Starlink has been a crucial tool for Ukraine's military since Russia's invasion in 2022 Image: NurPhoto/IMAGO Advertisement Polish officials on Monday said that two Turkish citizens have been detained in Germany in connection with a fire last month at a Starlink station in Poland . The satellite-based Starlink internet service is widely used by the military of Poland's neighbor Ukraine amid the Russian invasion . Officials from several EU countries have been warning of mounting Russian sabotage, cyber and hybrid attacks across Europe aiming either to erode support for Ukraine or to impact Ukraine directly. Polish officials did not specify exactly where or when the two men were allegedly detained in Germany. What did Poland say about the arrests and the case? Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski reported the arrests on Monday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk following soon after. "On behalf of Polish services, German police detained two Turkish citizens suspected of setting fire to a Starlink station in Masovia," he said on social media. "This is another act of hybrid warfare. The perpetrators of the sabotage will answer before the Polish justice system." Masovia is the province that includes the Polish capital Warsaw, not that far from Poland's eastern borders to Belarus and Ukraine. Poland blames Russia for incident Poland's Special Services Minister Tomasz Siemoniak alleged that Russia was behind the incident. He also told a press conference that, "​it is worth adding that Russian services are increasingly turning ​to individuals linked ‌to the criminal underworld" for such attacks. Russia typically dismisses European claims of hybrid warfare or systemic sabotage as either anti-Russian hysteria or disinformation. Will Elon Musk give Ukraine Starlink's eyes over Russia?
